title: Thread-safe logging
idea: A thread-safe logger writes each line as one indivisible unit, and an async appender lets many threads hand lines to one writer thread through a bounded queue.

analogy.text: A shared notebook. If two people alternate half-sentences, the page is garbage. Better: everyone drops finished notes in a tray, and one scribe copies them in.
analogy.breaks: A real tray never refuses notes; a full queue does.

points: Two writes per line let another thread slip in between, tearing the line.
Format the full line first, then write it in one locked call.
An async appender queues lines; one writer thread owns the output.
A bounded queue caps memory; here a full queue drops and counts, not blocks.

hero.title: Async appender with a bounded queue

steps.caption: An app thread calls `append(r1)`. `offer` puts it in the queue and returns at once.
The writer takes r1 and starts a slow disk write. The queue is empty again.
While the disk stalls, threads append r2 and r3. The queue is now full.
r4 arrives. `offer` returns false instead of blocking the request thread.
The appender counts r4 as dropped. A metric on that count tells operators.
The disk recovers. The writer finishes r1, then writes r2 and r3 in queue order.
`close` puts a STOP marker behind every line already queued; producers should stop before close, or a late line can land after STOP.
The writer takes STOP and exits. `close` joins it before returning.

code.title: Prove torn lines
code.caption: A barrier forces the bad interleaving every run. A thread-safe buffer does not help when one line takes two calls.

walk.text: A good line has one prefix and the same thread name in its body.
Each thread writes its prefix, waits for the other, then writes its body.
Both lines come out mangled, though every single append was thread-safe.
Fix: build the whole line, then append it once. The lock matters only for unsafe streams.
Start the threads, then join them all before counting lines.

code.title: Async appender
code.caption: Many producers, one writer thread, a bounded queue, a drop counter and a clean shutdown.

walk.text: Three threads append 200 lines each into a queue of 1000.
`close` drains everything; order per thread holds; late lines are refused.
A stalled disk and a queue of 2: the extra lines are dropped, not blocked.
The single writer thread loops on `take` until it sees STOP.
`offer` never waits: a full queue means drop and count.
`put` waits for space, so STOP lands after every queued line.

pitfalls: Never write prefix and message in separate calls to a shared stream.
Do not use an unbounded queue; a slow disk then eats all memory.
Always close the async appender on shutdown, or queued lines are lost.

quiz.q: What is the last line AsyncAppender prints?
options: It changes from run to run
quiz.why: The writer is stuck holding r1, so the queue starts empty. r2 and r3 fill both slots; `offer` refuses r4 and r5.

takeaway: One line, one write; many producers, one writer, a bounded queue.

starters: When should ERROR lines block instead of being dropped?
Why is a single writer thread simpler than locking the file?
What happens to queued lines if the JVM is killed with SIGKILL?
